question: For good body position, the manual recommends sitting far enough forward that your arms are slightly bent when holding the handgrips. Why?
choice_a: Bent arms let you press on the handlebars without having to reach too far
choice_b: It makes the motorcycle look sportier
choice_c: It reduces wind resistance at highway speed
choice_d: It keeps the throttle from sticking
explanation: Sit far enough forward so your arms are slightly bent when you hold the handgrips; bending your arms permits you to press on the handlebars without having to reach too far.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.9, 'Body Position'

question: Why does the manual recommend starting with your right wrist flat on the throttle?
choice_b: It helps keep you from accidentally using too much throttle
choice_c: It makes the horn easier to reach
choice_d: It is required for ABS to function
explanation: Hold the handgrips firmly and start with your right wrist flat -- this will help keep you from accidentally using too much throttle.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.9, 'Body Position'

question: Why should a rider keep their knees against the gas tank?
choice_a: It has no real safety purpose
choice_b: To keep the tank from overheating
choice_c: To help maintain balance as the motorcycle turns
explanation: Keep your knees against the gas tank to help you keep your balance as the motorcycle turns.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.9, 'Body Position'

question: Why does the manual warn against letting your toes point downward on the footrests?
choice_a: It only matters for passengers, not operators
choice_d: Toes pointed down may get caught between the road and the footrests
explanation: Keep your feet firmly on the footrests to maintain balance, and don't let your toes point downward -- they may get caught between the road and the footrests.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.9, 'Body Position'

question: On a typical motorcycle gear pattern of 1-N-2-3-4-5, how is neutral selected?
choice_a: By a half lift from 1st gear or a half press from 2nd gear
choice_b: By pressing the shift lever all the way down from 1st gear
choice_c: By lifting the shift lever twice from 1st gear
choice_d: Neutral cannot be selected while stopped
explanation: A typical gear pattern is 1-N-2-3-4-5. Neutral (N) is selected by either a half lift from 1st gear or a half press from 2nd gear.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.9, 'Shifting Gears'

question: What is the correct 3-step process for upshifting?
choice_a: Squeeze the clutch, roll on the throttle, then release the clutch suddenly
choice_b: Roll off the throttle while squeezing the clutch, lift the shift lever firmly and release, then smoothly ease out the clutch and adjust the throttle
choice_c: Press the shift lever down, release the clutch instantly, then apply the rear brake
choice_d: Roll on the throttle fully before touching the clutch at all
explanation: When upshifting: 1) roll off the throttle as you squeeze the clutch lever, 2) lift the shift lever firmly as far as it will go and release, 3) smoothly ease out the clutch lever and adjust the throttle.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.9, 'Shifting Gears'

question: What effect is created when a rider shifts to a lower gear and eases out the clutch to slow the motorcycle?
explanation: Shifting to a lower gear causes an effect similar to using the brakes, known as engine braking. To use it, shift down one gear at a time and ease out the clutch lever through the friction zone between each downshift.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.9, 'Shifting Gears'

question: Why should a rider remain in first gear while stopped?
choice_a: It is the only gear that engages the brake light
choice_b: It is required to keep the engine from stalling
choice_d: So the motorcycle can move out quickly if needed
explanation: Remain in first gear while you are stopped so that you can move out quickly if you need to.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.9, 'Shifting Gears'

question: The front brake can provide how much of a motorcycle's total stopping power?
explanation: Most motorcycles have two brake controls, one for the front wheel and one for the rear. The front brake is more powerful and can provide 70% or more of total stopping power, and is safe to use if used properly.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.10, 'Braking'

question: How is maximum straight-line braking accomplished?
choice_a: By using only the rear brake
choice_b: By fully applying both front and rear brakes without locking either wheel
choice_c: By using only the front brake
choice_d: By coasting in neutral with no brakes applied
explanation: Maximum straight-line braking is accomplished by fully applying both front and rear brakes without locking either wheel.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.10, 'Braking'

question: As a motorcycle's weight transfers forward during braking, what happens to available traction at the front wheel?
choice_a: Traction shifts entirely to the rear wheel
choice_b: Traction disappears completely at the front wheel
choice_c: More traction becomes available, so the front brake can be applied more firmly
choice_d: Traction is unaffected by weight transfer
explanation: As the motorcycle's weight transfers forward, more traction becomes available at the front wheel, so the front brake can be applied more firmly after braking begins.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.10, 'Braking'

question: Why does the manual recommend using both brakes even for normal, everyday stops?
choice_a: It has no benefit beyond looking more professional
choice_b: Using only one brake will damage the transmission
choice_c: State law requires both brakes for every stop
choice_d: It develops the proper skill of using both brakes together for an emergency stop
explanation: Using both brakes for even normal stops permits you to develop the proper skill of using both brakes properly in an emergency; grabbing the front brake or jamming the rear can cause the brakes to lock.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.10, 'Braking'

question: What happens to available traction for braking as lean angle increases in a curve?
choice_a: It decreases -- the greater the lean angle, the more likely the tires are to lose traction
choice_c: Lean angle has no effect on traction
choice_d: Traction only matters for the rear tire in a curve
explanation: Any time a motorcycle is leaned over, the amount of traction available for braking is reduced. The greater the lean angle, the greater the possibility of the tires losing traction.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.10, 'Braking in a Corner'

question: An anti-lock braking system (ABS) is designed to:
choice_b: Prevent wheel lock-up and avoid skids when stopping in panic situations
choice_c: Replace the need for a front brake entirely
explanation: ABS is designed to prevent wheel lock-up and avoid skids when stopping in panic situations; if sensors detect a possible wheel lock, brake pressure is released then reapplied, more than 15 times per second, to maintain maximum braking effectiveness.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.10, 'Anti-Lock Braking Systems (ABS)'

question: In a linked braking system, what happens when the rider applies either the front lever or the rear pedal?
choice_b: Only the brake actually operated is applied, exactly like an unlinked system
choice_c: Braking pressure is applied to both brakes
explanation: Linked braking connects the front and rear brakes and applies braking pressure to both brakes when either the front lever or rear pedal is applied. An integrated system additionally applies partial front braking whenever the rear brake is activated.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.10, 'Linked and Integrated Braking Systems'

question: What is the correct four-step sequence for turning effectively?
explanation: The four steps to turn effectively are SLOW (reduce speed before the turn), LOOK (look through the turn to where you want to go), PRESS (press the handgrip in the direction of the turn to lean), and ROLL (roll on the throttle to stabilize).
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.10-11, 'Turning'

question: To turn left on a motorcycle, which handgrip should the rider press, and in what direction should the motorcycle lean?
choice_a: Press the left handgrip, leaning left
choice_b: Press the right handgrip, leaning left
choice_c: Press the left handgrip, leaning right
choice_d: Pull back on both handgrips equally
explanation: To turn, the motorcycle must lean. Press the left handgrip to lean left and go left; press the right handgrip to lean right and go right.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.11, 'Turning'

question: In slow, tight turns, how should a rider position their body relative to the leaning motorcycle?
choice_a: Lean the body at the same angle as the motorcycle
choice_b: Counterbalance by leaning the motorcycle only and keeping the body upright
choice_c: Lean the body more than the motorcycle
explanation: In regular turns, the rider and motorcycle should lean together at the same angle. In slow, tight turns, counterbalance by leaning the motorcycle only and keeping your body upright.
source_note: MN DPS Motorcycle and Motorized Bicycle Manual (PS30001-21, 11/2021), p.11, 'Turning'
